subject: snail
pitch: A garden snail on an adventure. A glossy spiral shell striped in caramel, chocolate and cream, a soft grey-green body with a pebbly texture and a slimy shine, two long eye stalks with little black eyes and two short feelers below. A tiny ladybird hitches a ride on top of the shell.
reasoning:
I'm planning a three.js module for a garden snail, scaled around 0.2m long, with a spiral-striped shell built from a lathe geometry following a logarithmic curve, plus a body, eye stalks, feelers, and a ladybird perched on top.

Simpler plan: build the shell as a series of decreasing ellipsoid whorls stacked along a spiral path, with banded torus rings for colored stripes, rather than a textured lathe surface. I'm laying out coordinates with the snail facing +Z, an elongated foot body, and the shell positioned toward the back, sketching out the whorl sizes and placement.

For stripes, I think a canvas texture is cleaner than vertex colors since it avoids hard edges unless bands align with vertices — I'll generate a small canvas with color bands, set it to repeat, and map the UV coordinate along the shell's spiral path to pick up the correct stripe.

I'll settle on mapping colour to v so the texture stripes wrap around the tube cross-section, giving the look of spiral banding on the coil, and map that onto canvas y with flipY applied. I'll also add glossiness via MeshPhysicalMaterial with clearcoat for a wet shell look.

For the shell geometry itself, I'm defining a conical helix: center position moves outward and upward while radius R(t) shrinks exponentially with turns, and the tube radius shrinks proportionally too — but since snail shells overlap in a flatter coil, I'm simplifying to a vertical-axis helix with small pitch and tube radius around 0.022, radius tapering from 0.05 to 0.012.

Actually a gently rising spiral with increasing height reads more like a real dome-shaped shell, so I'll go with that tilted-cone approach and keep the implementation simple and robust.

I'm building a tube generator along a path with computed tangent/normal frames (using a reference up vector to construct the normal, avoiding degeneracies), producing geometry with proper normals and UVs. For the shell path itself, I'm coiling around the Y axis through about 2.6 turns with the radius shrinking exponentially as the coil winds inward.

Adjusting the radius and height falloff so the spiral forms a cone-shaped spire rising to an apex, with the wider body whorl at the base -- matching a typical snail shell shape. I'm placing the shell toward the back of the body, roughly centered above and behind, with a base radius around 0.075 and total height about 0.07, scaled relative to an overall snail length.

Reconsidering the real-world scale -- garden snail shells are only a few centimeters across, so I'm shrinking the shell radius down to about 0.028 and the snail body to around 0.12, with the tiny ladybird around 7mm, erring toward readability over strict realism. I'm tuning the tube radius and per-turn spacing so the coils overlap properly without gaps.

Now I'm positioning the shell relative to the body -- setting the group translation so it sits above the foot, and tilting it backward slightly around the X axis so the spire leans back the way a real snail's shell naturally angles.

Still placing body parts...

For the materials, I'm planning a speckled CanvasTexture for the body with a bump map, and using MeshPhysicalMaterial with clearcoat for a slimy sheen. Then I'm starting on the eye stalks using tube geometry.

Now I'm adding eye stalks with CatmullRom curves curling upward, tiny black eyes with white highlight dots, and shorter feeler tubes positioned below them. I'm also planning a small ladybird perched near the top of the shell's spiral, with a red segmented body and a black dividing line.

Still working out the ladybird's head and spots as small black spheres, and positioning a dome-shaped shell top near where the spiral apex converges close to the central axis.

I'll compute the position from the same spiral function and offset it slightly upward so the ladybird rests on the tube's surface, though I should double check whether "up" aligns with the actual tube normal given the spiral's orientation.

I'm placing the ladybird around s=0.3 along the tube, parenting it to the shell group so it inherits the spiral's motion, and giving it a slight rotation so it faces forward naturally. For scale, I'm sizing the ladybird's body to roughly match real-world proportions (~7mm), checking that it fits comfortably against the tube radius at that point on the spiral.

Now I'm building out the ladybird's anatomy: a red flattened-sphere body sitting slightly sunk into position, a small black head sphere up front, a thin dark midline seam along the back, and a handful of flattened black spots scattered across the red elytra for the classic ladybird look.

For the shell's texture, I'm working through how the canvas-based stripe pattern should map onto the tube's UV space — since the bands on a real snail shell wrap around each whorl along the spiral path rather than running lengthwise, I need the stripe pattern to vary with position along the path rather than around the tube's circumference.

I'll settle on a simple striped texture with repeat wrapping, then move to a pebbly body texture using grey-green noise with speckles as both map and bump map for the body spheres sharing a material. Now I'm sketching out the tube geometry function that builds position and UV arrays along a path with variable radius and segment counts.

Writing tube generator code...

Checking the vertical spacing per turn against tube diameter — each turn rises about 0.0135 while the tube diameter is around 0.016, so consecutive coils will overlap rather than leave visible gaps, which should look fine.

I'm figuring out the cone-like taper of the spiral: radius shrinks while height climbs, giving the shell its sloped profile, with the body whorl thicker near the base. I'm settling on roughly 260 path segments across 2.6 turns and 14 radial segments, giving a mesh of a few thousand vertices, and defining a radius function that tapers from about 0.012 down as the parameter increases.

Now I'm positioning the shell within the overall body, checking that its base sinks properly into the mantle sphere so the geometry reads as one cohesive snail, and working out the overall height and width so the proportions look right. I'm building out the body parts next -- the foot, mantle hump, head, snout, and tail -- each as scaled spheres placed at specific offsets to form a convincing creature.

For the eyes, I'm constructing curved stalks using tube geometry along Catmull-Rom curves, topped with tiny black eyeballs with a small white highlight for shine, plus separate thinner feeler stalks in the body color. Finally I'm defining the materials: a textured grey-green physical material for the body and a striped clearcoat material for the shell.

I'm setting up the color palette (caramel, chocolate, cream tones) and generating a canvas texture with horizontal stripe bands, plus a separate noisy body texture with random speckles used for both color and bump mapping, repeated via texture wrapping and driven by a seeded random generator. Now I'm positioning a ladybird detail as a child of the shell, placed along a curve point offset by the shell's radius.

Working out the ladybird's orientation and placement...

Working out the ellipsoid scaling for spot placement...

I'll place 6 small spots total, mirrored across the x-axis, using slightly embedded spheres of radius 0.0008 at varied positions along the body. Then I'm adding the head as a black ellipsoid sphere scaled and positioned at the front of the body.

Now I'm adding a thin midline divider box, giving the body a glossy clearcoat material to suggest a sheen, and setting up a canvas helper function for texture generation.

For the shell, I'm painting a banded texture onto a small canvas—alternating cream, caramel, and chocolate stripes of varying widths—then wrapping it as a CanvasTexture so the colors cycle radially around the coil.

Now I'm setting up a separate body texture: a 256px canvas with scattered noise dots and darker pebble-like spots to give the snail's skin a subtle grainy, speckled look, which I'll reuse as a bump map for surface roughness.

Still generating body texture noise...

Drawing banded color stripes for the shell texture...

Now I'm defining the shell's physical material with clearcoat and roughness for a glossy finish, and setting up the texture coordinates so the vertical band pattern maps correctly around the tube. I'm also starting to assemble the material set, including a standard material for the eyes.

Writing tube geometry function...

Finalizing buffer attributes and normals, then defining the spiral shell path as a helix function with 2.6 turns, using radial segments of 14 and 240 length segments before creating the shell mesh.

I'm positioning and rotating the shell group so its apex tilts backward, then placing the ladybird on the shell surface at a fixed point along the path, orienting it using the tangent direction to align with the spiral's curve.

So different coil turns don't land at the same angle, which is good. Now I'm working out the ladybird's position relative to the tube's radius and building its body as a small scaled sphere group, positioning it so it sits slightly nestled into the tube surface rather than floating above it.

Still writing ladybird details...

Adding the highlight offset and tiny feeler tubes with tip spheres, then assembling the full snail group with body, shell, and eyes, making sure the lowest body point touches the ground.
